explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The king settled them in the towns of Samaria, and they took possession and lived there. Five different places of origin, one region. I think that's a lot of new neighbors to get used to.

explanations.answer: In the cities of the Medes
explanations.explanation: The Medes are close, friend, but that's a different move. The cities of the Medes are where some of the Israelites ended up when they were carried off (2 Kings 17:6). The new people were settled in Samaria to replace them. Two groups, opposite directions.

explanations.answer: In Gozan by the Habor River
explanations.explanation: Gozan by the Habor River is on the other side of this move, baker. That's one of the places the Israelites were settled when they were carried off (2 Kings 17:6). The settlers in this passage went the other way, into the towns of Samaria. Two groups, two directions.

explanations.answer: We don't know what the God of the land requires
explanations.explanation: That's what they told the king. They said the peoples he had moved in did not know the requirements of the God of the land, and the lions were killing them off. Notice they're not blaming the weather or the neighborhood. They name the God of the land and what they don't know about Him. That's a real report, friend.

explanations.answer: Our towns don't have walls to keep them out
explanations.explanation: Walls never come up in what they say, baker. Their report to the king is about the requirements of the God of the land, which they don't know. The lions are killing them off, and that's the reason they give. A wall would be a nice idea, but nobody in this passage asks for one.

explanations.answer: The land sat empty and wild for far too long
explanations.explanation: That's a reasonable guess, but it's not what they say. Their words to the king are that the peoples don't know the requirements of the God of the land, and the lions are killing them off. Nothing about the land sitting empty. It's a heavy part of the story, friend, and the settlers name the real reason they gave.

explanations.answer: One of the priests carried off from Samaria
explanations.explanation: You've got it. The king commands them to send back one of the priests they carried off from Samaria to live there and teach. Think about that, friend. The king reaches back into the group he took away to find the teacher. Somebody's getting a very surprising travel notice.

explanations.answer: One of the prophets living in Judah
explanations.explanation: Prophets aren't in the king's command, baker. He says to send back one of the priests carried off from Samaria. The priest is the one who goes back to live there and teach. Different job title, different order.

explanations.answer: One of his own officials from Assyria
explanations.explanation: The king doesn't pick one of his own officials. He commands them to send back one of the priests they carried off from Samaria. That's the person who is supposed to go live there and teach. The teacher comes from the priests, baker, not from the king's staff.

Close, friend, but the verse names a different town. The text says the priest came and lived in Bethel, not Jerusalem. Jerusalem never comes up in this part of the passage. Same land, different address.

False is right, baker. The priest came and lived in Bethel, and he began to teach them how they should worship the LORD. Jerusalem isn't in this scene at all. I'd like to remind everybody that I got sent to a drawer, not a town, and I still found my way.

Gods, baker. The people of each nation kept making their own gods in the cities where they settled, even with a priest teaching them. That's not a small side project. It's a heavy thing, and the text says it plainly.

Laws sounds right, but the verse says they made their own gods. The priest was teaching them how to worship the LORD, and they kept making gods in the cities where they had settled. Making gods is a different thing than writing laws. Close pick, friend.

Towns aren't what they kept making, baker. The settlers lived in the towns of Samaria, and the verse says they made their own gods in the cities where they had settled. The answer is gods. Close pick, friend.

explanations.answer: In the shrines on the high places
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. They set up their gods in the shrines on the high places, the ones the people of Samaria had made. So they moved into places someone else had already built. Free real estate, wrong use of it.

Jerusalem isn't mentioned here, baker. The text says they set their gods up in the shrines that the people of Samaria had made on the high places. That's where the gods went. Not the temple, and not a place anyone should have put them.

Dagon is a Philistine god, and his temple turns up in a different story (1 Samuel 5:2). Here, the gods went into the shrines that the people of Samaria had made on the high places. Different gods, different shrines. Easy mix-up when so many names fly by.

Yes, baker. They worshiped the LORD, but they also appointed for themselves priests of all sorts to serve in the shrines of the high places. Not one priest. All sorts. That's like getting a whole bakery's worth of bakers without ever checking who's in charge of the oven.

The priest at Bethel is the one who taught them how to worship the LORD (2 Kings 17:28). But verse 32 says they appointed priests of all sorts for themselves. Not only him. The word "only" is what trips this one up, friend.
Levites and Jerusalem don't show up in this verse, baker. The text says they appointed for themselves priests of all sorts. They did the choosing. Careful with that word "only."

Customs is it. They worshiped the LORD, but they also served their own gods according to the customs of the nations from which they had been carried away. They kept the old habits from back home. I've kept habits too long myself, friend, and mine were just about cookie sizes.

Kings are not what the verse says, baker. It says they served their own gods according to the customs of the nations they were carried away from. Customs, meaning the way things were done back home. Nobody's naming a king here.

Armies don't come up, friend. The verse says they served their own gods according to the customs of the nations from which they had been carried away. It's about how they did things, not who marched. The answer is customs.

That's the first command, baker. The LORD commanded the Israelites, "Do not worship other gods or bow down to them; do not serve them or sacrifice to them." (2 Kings 17:35). Notice how that one line covers worship, bowing, serving and sacrificing. It's the very thing the settlers were doing in the shrines.

explanations.answer: Do not ever leave the land
explanations.explanation: Leaving the land isn't in the command, friend. Verse 35 starts with "Do not worship other gods or bow down to them…" (2 Kings 17:35). That's the first thing He tells them. The land isn't even the topic of that line.

explanations.answer: Do not trade with the nations
explanations.explanation: Trading isn't in the command, baker. What He says first is, "Do not worship other gods or bow down to them…" (2 Kings 17:35). That one's about who they worship, not who they do business with. Easy pick, but not the one.

True, baker. He told them, "You are to bow down to Him and offer sacrifices to Him." (2 Kings 17:36). That comes right after reminding them He brought them out of Egypt with great power and an outstretched arm. Who rescued them and who they bow to go together.

It's actually true, friend. The verse says, "You are to bow down to Him and offer sacrifices to Him." (2 Kings 17:36). He says it right after He reminds them He brought them out of Egypt. So bowing and sacrificing to Him are exactly what He tells them to do.

explanations.answer: He will deliver them from all their enemies
explanations.explanation: That's the promise, baker. He says to worship the LORD their God, "…and He will deliver you from the hands of all your enemies." (2 Kings 17:39). Look at the pairing. First He says to worship Him alone, then He tells them what He'll do. That's a promise worth holding onto.

explanations.answer: He will give them a king who rules forever
explanations.explanation: A king who rules forever isn't what this verse promises, friend. What He says here is that He will deliver them from the hands of all their enemies (2 Kings 17:39). That's the promise tied to worshiping Him. Stay with the text on this one.

explanations.answer: He will send them rain in every season
explanations.explanation: Rain isn't part of this promise, baker. In these verses He says that if they worship the LORD their God, He will deliver them from the hands of all their enemies (2 Kings 17:39). That's what's on the table. I'd take rain too, but it isn't here.
Not quite, friend. The text says the opposite. To this day their children and grandchildren continue to do as their fathers did. The habit got passed down, not broken.

False is right, baker. The nations worshiped the LORD but also served their idols, and to this day their children and grandchildren continue to do as their fathers did. The habit rolled right down the family line. It's easier to hand down a recipe than a change of heart.
